England have since played three games in Spain, although they refused to return to Madrid for the first of them in 2009. The match was moved to Seville. guardianfootball.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
guardianfootball.description: Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player . You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses…

quietus.title: The Strange World of… Suzanne Ciani
quietus.description: In her eightieth year, during her first ever trip to Scotland to close Sonica festival in Glasgow, electronic music pioneer Suzanne Ciani looks back on her career with Claire Sawers. Main portrait: Dan Wilton From her early days studying classical composition, to her game-changing friendship with the electronic instrument designer Don Buchla, Suzanne Ciani was always interested in world building. Her ability to create vast, echoing dreamscapes or equally impactful sonic miniatures has gained her huge respect and a broad, multi-generational fanbase; one that didn’t exist at the outset, as the technologies she used were initially only known to a handful. Ciani persevered with her progressive…

So, imagine my delight when the new Tara Cunningham record, Warm Ground, described in the presser as a…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Marshall Crenshaw :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: With his crystal clear voice and keen melodic sensibility, Marshall Crenshaw stands as one of the finest rock songwriters going. His latest collection, The Bootleg Sounds of Marshall Crenshaw: 1984-1987 , offers a peek into his process. Culled from his extensive archives, the record brings together unreleased demos, live cuts, and unheard studio recordings captured in the lead up to his third and fourth LPs, 1985's Downtown and 1987's Mary Jean & 9 Others . Full of scuffed up, lo-fi charm, it's a testament to Crenshaw that even his rough drafts feel like brillant slices of pop rock.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Habibi Funk 035 :: Beirut City Pop
aquariumdrunkard.description: In a departure from the usual template of old photos of the artists, the cover of Habibi Funk’s latest reissue features an illustration by Beirut-born, Paris-based artist Raphaelle Macaron. Poolside beach chairs sit empty on the patio of a luxurious apartment complex at dusk, separated by red, rocky terrain from the city skyline in the background. Cool purples, pinks and blues saturate the scene in a clear nod to the style of Hiroshi Nagai, whose work graces the covers of Light in the Attic’s Pacific Breeze City Pop compilations of funk, soul and AOR from 1980’s Japan. But while the references in the album’s title and cover art lovingly highlight the parallels with the City Pop era, the…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Linus + Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy :: The Outsider: The Music of Jules Decorte
aquariumdrunkard.description: Three oddly-shaped pieces come together in the most natural way in this under-the-radar release from Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy. The disc reconfigures the work of blind Dutch songwriter Jules de Corte, an outsider artist who wrote and recorded over 3,000 songs during his lifetime. This is not what you’d call a natural fit. De Corte’s songs are quick and witty and cerebral, more like cabaret or art song than BPB’s mournful Americana. Yet the two artists share an unconventional spirituality; there’s real searching in De Corte’s cleverly put together tunes.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Lex Walton :: Ultimate Love Forever
aquariumdrunkard.description: Lex Walton makes swaggering, theatrical, large-scale rock - the spit and snarl of her vocals punk laced, the instrumental arrangements swelling to arena-rock proportions. Dan Boeckner, half of one of the last big emotive rock duos of the aughts and teens, produced Ultimate Love Forever , and it has, sonically at least, some of Wolf Parade’s unabashed romanticism. The content is lacerating, the mood nihilistic, but the music itself is all about the good time. It high-kicks and cake-walks and vibrates with theatrical music hall energies.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Adam Voith
aquariumdrunkard.description: Our guest this week is author Adam Voith, whose new novel, RIYL , short for "Recommended If You Like," is an at times thinly veiled memoir of the '90s Christian punk and indie scene. With echoes of Get in the Van and Freaks and Geeks, RIYL threads that delicate needle of looking back at earnest teenage corn doggery with warts and all embarrassment, tempered by the type of affection that only time and distance allow all of us. It's also frequently flat out hilarious.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Hiroshi Yoshimura :: Quiet Forest
aquariumdrunkard.description: With no deceleration in sight, the 2020s have thus far been the decade of Kankyō Ongaku pioneer Hiroshi Yoshimura. 1996's Quiet Forest , the musician's final offering, is another gem in a slew of reissues courtesy of tireless label Temporal Drift. The Hoh Rainforest is the setting here, as Yoshimura interprets the terrain with his singular approach: superimposed synth soundscapes that contagiously mirror the greenery and precipitation: fluttering new age soundscapes as opulent as they are evocative.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Ronnie Self :: The Lost Sessions
aquariumdrunkard.description: Best remembered for the unhinged rockabilly of “Bop-a-Lena” and Brenda Lee’s “I’m Sorry,” Ronnie Self spent much of his later career writing songs that went largely unheard. The Lost Sessions , a collection of seventeen recordings from that period, finds him somewhere between country, folk-rock, and the lonely hours of the night. A long-overdue glimpse of the songwriter behind the legend.

mubi.title: The Possibilities of the Unseen: In Conversation with Lee Chang-dong
mubi.description: Lee Chang-dong. When I first met Lee Chang-dong in person, in April 2025, he was already waiting for me at his office in Seoul’s Mapo District. He sat hunched over his notes, reviewing the questions I had sent him in advance. After a moment of small talk, he looked up at me, his expression suddenly serious. “How long do you want to talk?” he asked. I thought two hours would be enough. “Not enough,” he replied. We talked for nearly four hours, with a large Secret Sunshine (2007) poster looming behind us. Our conversation took place in Seoul ahead of a retrospective of Lee’s work at Poland’s New Horizons Film Festival. He couldn’t attend in person, as he was busy finishing Possible Love…
